findings.title: AI threats in the wild: The current state of prompt injections on the web
findings.summary: Posted by Thomas Brunner, Yu-Han Liu, Moni Pande At Google, our Threat Intelligence teams are dedicated to staying ahead of real-world adversarial activity, proactively monitoring emerging threats before they can impact users. Right now, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) is a top priority for the security community, anticipating it as a primary attack vector for adversaries to target and compromise AI agents. But while the danger of IPI is widely discussed, are threat actors actually exploiting this vector today – and if so, how? To answer these questions and to uncover real-world abuse, we initiated a broad sweep of the public web to monitor for known indirect prompt injection patterns. This is what we found. The threat of indirect prompt injection Unlike a direct injection where a user "jailbreaks" a chatbot, IPI occurs when an AI system processes content—like a website, email, or document—that contains malicious instructions. When the AI reads this poisoned content, it may silently follow the attacker's commands instead of the user's original intent. This is not a new area of concern for us and Google has been working tirelessly to combat these threats. Our efforts involve cross-functional collaboration between researchers at Google DeepMind (GDM) and defenders like the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG). We have previously detailed our work in this area and researchers have further highlighted the evolving nature of these vulnerabilities. Despite this collective focus, a fundamental question remains: to what degree are real-world malicious actors currently operationalizing these attacks? Proactive monitoring at Google The landscape of IPI on the web There are many channels through which attackers might try to send prompt injections. However, one location is particularly easy to observe - the public web. Here, threat actors may simply seed prompt injections on websites in hope of corrupting AI systems that browse them. findings.title: Google Workspace’s continuous approach to mitigating indirect prompt injections
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team Indirect prompt injection (IPI) is an evolving threat vector targeting users of complex AI applications with multiple data sources, such as Workspace with Gemini. This technique enables the attacker to influence the behavior of an LLM by injecting malicious instructions into the data or tools used by the LLM as it completes the user’s query. This may even be possible without any input directly from the user. IPI is not the kind of technical problem you “solve” and move on. Sophisticated LLMs with increasing use of agentic automation combined with a wide range of content create an ultra-dynamic and evolving playground for adversarial attacks. That’s why Google takes a sophisticated and comprehensive approach to these attacks. We’re continuously improving LLM resistance to IPI attacks and launching AI application capabilities with ever-improving defenses. Staying ahead of the latest indirect prompt injection attacks is critical to our mission of securing Workspace with Gemini. In our previous blog “ Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy ”, we reviewed the layered architecture of our IPI defenses. In this blog, we’ll share more detail on the continuous approach we take to improve these defenses and to solve for new attacks. New attack discovery By proactively discovering and cataloging new attack vectors through internal and external programs, we can identify vulnerabilities and deploy robust defenses ahead of adversarial activity. findings.title: Architecting Security for Agentic Capabilities in Chrome
findings.summary: Posted by Nathan Parker, Chrome security team Chrome has been advancing the web’s security for well over 15 years, and we’re committed to meeting new challenges and opportunities with AI. Billions of people trust Chrome to keep them safe by default, and this is a responsibility we take seriously. Following the recent launch of Gemini in Chrome and the preview of agentic capabilities , we want to share our approach and some new innovations to improve the safety of agentic browsing. The primary new threat facing all agentic browsers is indirect prompt injection . It can appear in malicious sites, third-party content in iframes, or from user-generated content like user reviews, and can cause the agent to take unwanted actions such as initiating financial transactions or exfiltrating sensitive data. Given this open challenge, we are investing in a layered defense that includes both deterministic and probabilistic defenses to make it difficult and costly for attackers to cause harm. Designing safe agentic browsing for Chrome has involved deep collaboration of security experts across Google. We built on Gemini's existing protections and agent security principles and have implemented several new layers for Chrome. We’re introducing a user alignment critic where the agent’s actions are vetted by a separate model that is isolated from untrusted content. We’re also extending Chrome’s origin-isolation capabilities to constrain what origins the agent can interact with, to just those that are relevant to the task. Our layered defense also includes user confirmations for critical steps, real-time detection of threats , and red-teaming and response . We’ll step through these layers below. findings.title: Rust in Android: move fast and fix things
findings.summary: Posted by Jeff Vander Stoep, Android Last year, we wrote about why a memory safety strategy that focuses on vulnerability prevention in new code quickly yields durable and compounding gains. This year we look at how this approach isn’t just fixing things, but helping us move faster . The 2025 data continues to validate the approach, with memory safety vulnerabilities falling below 20% of total vulnerabilities for the first time. Updated data for 2025. This data covers first-party and third-party (open source) code changes to the Android platform across C, C++, Java, Kotlin, and Rust. This post is published a couple of months before the end of 2025, but Android’s industry-standard 90-day patch window means that these results are very likely close to final. We can and will accelerate patching when necessary. We adopted Rust for its security and are seeing a 1000x reduction in memory safety vulnerability density compared to Android’s C and C++ code . But the biggest surprise was Rust's impact on software delivery. With Rust changes having a 4x lower rollback rate and spending 25% less time in code review , the safer path is now also the faster one. findings.title: Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team With the rapid adoption of generative AI, a new wave of threats is emerging across the industry with the aim of manipulating the AI systems themselves. One such emerging attack vector is indirect prompt injections. Unlike direct prompt injections, where an attacker directly inputs malicious commands into a prompt, indirect prompt injections involve hidden malicious instructions within external data sources. These may include emails, documents, or calendar invites that instruct AI to exfiltrate user data or execute other rogue actions. As more governments, businesses, and individuals adopt generative AI to get more done, this subtle yet potentially potent attack becomes increasingly pertinent across the industry, demanding immediate attention and robust security measures. At Google, our teams have a longstanding precedent of investing in a defense-in-depth strategy, including robust evaluation, threat analysis, AI security best practices , AI red-teaming , adversarial training, and model hardening for generative AI tools. This approach enables safer adoption of Gemini in Google Workspace and the Gemini app (we refer to both in this blog as “Gemini” for simplicity). Below we describe our prompt injection mitigation product strategy based on extensive research, development, and deployment of improved security mitigations. A layered security approach Google has taken a layered security approach introducing security measures designed for each stage of the prompt lifecycle. From Gemini 2.5 model hardening, to purpose-built machine learning (ML) models detecting malicious instructions, to system-level safeguards, we are meaningfully elevating the difficulty, expense, and complexity faced by an attacker. This approach compels adversaries to resort to methods that are either more easily identified or demand greater resources. Our model training with adversarial data significantly enhanced our defenses against indirect prompt

findings.title: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite
findings.summary: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite Executive summary A group of Russian state-supported cyber actors has been targeting and compromising various Western government and commercial organizations using the Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) software since at least July 2025. The Russian state-supported advanced persistent threat (APT) group’s activity is tracked in the cybersecurity community under several names (see Cybersecurity industry tracking ), primarily as “LAUNDRY BEAR,” a name initially coined by the Netherlands General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) and Defence Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) [ 1 ]. LAUNDRY BEAR’s targeting is almost certainly to gather sensitive information for the Russian Federation, with these actors primarily focusing on the covert acquisition of email data. Previous campaigns indicated LAUNDRY BEAR relied on unsophisticated initial access techniques—including password spraying, phishing, and pass-the-cookie—allowing the group to successfully run high-volume operations. The latest campaign targeting ZCS uses a novel exploit that was a zero-day vulnerability when first exploited and continues to be successfully exploited. The vulnerability, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) CVE-2025-66376 , was patched in November 2025. This demonstrates LAUNDRY BEAR’s intent and ability to deploy increasingly sophisticated technical capabilities. Unlike traditional phishing campaigns that persuade a user into taking an action, such as clicking a link or opening a file, LAUNDRY BEAR’s latest campaign leverages a view-based exploit that only requires a user to view a malicious email within a vulnerable version of the webmail service. Once viewed, the exploit attempts to exfiltrate the victim’s last 90 days of email communications, the organization email directory (i.e., Global Address List [GAL]), and other sensitive information to servers controlled by LAUN

findings.title: Happy DOM: Incomplete fix for CVE-2026-33943: unsanitized import alias leads to host code execution
findings.summary:
## Summary

The ESM compiler in `happy-dom@20.14.5` does not validate imported local binding aliases before interpolating them into generated JavaScript.

As a result, an invalid ESM import alias can be transformed into a valid JavaScript destructuring default initializer and executed.

This appears to be an alternate injection path and incomplete remediation of GHSA-6q6h-j7hj-3r64 / CVE-2026-33943. The previous fix validates `importName` in the local `export { ... }` handler, but the named import handler still places an unvalidated `alias` directly into code context.

These issues were confirmed through the public `Window` and `<script type="module">` APIs using the published `happy-dom` npm package. The PoC reaches the Node.js host `process`, obtains `node:fs`, and creates a proof directory on the host filesystem.

## Confirmed affected versions

The PoC was directly tested against:

- `happy-dom@17.0.0`
- `happy-dom@20.0.0`
- `happy-dom@20.1.0`
- `happy-dom@20.14.5`

The same PoC does not trigger on `happy-dom@16.8.1`.

The ESM compiler was introduced by commit `7bc831df2`, first released in `v17.0.0`. The vulnerable interpolation remains present through `v20.14.5`, the latest release at the time of testing.

Suggested affected range:

```text
>= 17.0.0, <= 20.14.5
```

No patched version is currently available.

## Preconditions

- JavaScript evaluation is enabled with `enableJavaScriptEvaluation: true`.
- Attacker-controlled HTML or module source is processed by Happy DOM.
- This may affect SSR, preview, scraping, or testing services that evaluate externally supplied HTML.

## Technical details

In `packages/happy-dom/src/module/ECMAScriptModuleCompiler.ts`, the named import handler splits an import specifier and extracts its alias:

```ts
const nameParts = part.trim().split(/\s+as\s+/);
const alias = (nameParts[1] || nameParts[0]).replace(/["']/g, '');
const name = nameParts[0].replace(/["']/g, '');

if (alias && name) {
  properties.push({ name, alias });
}
`

findings.title: virtualenv: Bash prompt values can change meaning under older compatibility modes
findings.summary:
## Summary

Caller-supplied prompt text can become executable syntax in the bash activation prompt. An attacker must influence the
value passed to virtualenv, and a user must subsequently activate the environment and draw the prompt.

## Affected area

Bash runs with compatibility level 4.2 and draws the environment prompt. Its replacement-string behavior differs from
newer compatibility modes, leaving prompt text subject to a second interpretation. The report concerns POSIX activation.
It does not establish exposure through unrelated activators.

## Attacker-controlled input

The attacker controls prompt or destination data passed as a virtualenv argument. The user later sources the generated
activation script.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[bash prompt assembly](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/bash/activate.sh).

## Mechanism

`bin/activate` copies the prompt into `PS1`. A shell expands `PS1` again when it draws a prompt, so the value must
survive both the assignment and that later expansion. The bash and zsh branches escape for their usual prompt rules.
Three other paths still interpret prompt data as commands: dash sourcing `activate` directly, a child dash inheriting an
exported `PS1` from bash, and bash running at compatibility level 4.2 or lower. A value such as `x$(touch MARKER)y` then
runs `touch` on prompt display. Creating the environment does not run the payload.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner's child-shell reproducer creates an environment with `--prompt 'x$(touch MARKER)y'`, sources `bin/activate`
in interactive bash, and starts interactive `sh` (dash). Its control leaves `PS1` unexported: neither shell creates
`MARKER`. With `PS1` exported, bash displays the prompt without executing the value, but the child dash creates
`MARKER`; the reproducer ends in `BUG`. The report gives separate console reproductions for direct dash activation and
bash c

findings.title: undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unbounded memory in the EventSource parser
findings.summary:
### Impact

undici's `EventSource` client can be driven to exhaust process memory by a malicious or compromised Server-Sent Events peer. By sending millions of tiny completed `data:` fields with no blank event separator, or a single unfinished line split across many chunks, the parser retains a growing amount of per-field and per-chunk state. The byte-based `maxEventSize` and `maxResponseSize` limits do not bound that retained state, and `maxResponseSize` is enforced on the compressed body before decompression, so a small compressed response can expand into enough retained memory to terminate the process. The application only needs to maintain an `EventSource` connection to an untrusted peer, which controls only the response. Availability is the only impact.

### Patches

Upgrade to `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`, which bound the retained EventSource parser state (the number of `data` fields and buffered chunks, the unfinished-line length, and per-field byte totals) independently of the byte limits.

### Workarounds

None.

findings.title: MLflow: SSRF on unauthenticated MLflow servers via third-party scorer kwargs in the scorer invoke, register, and GenAI evaluate endpoints
findings.summary:
### Summary
MLflow's tracking server exposes `POST /ajax-api/3.0/mlflow/scorer/invoke` with **no authentication**, and the handler reflectively instantiates an attacker-named class from attacker-supplied JSON with unconstrained constructor kwargs. With the optional `trulens` + `trulens-providers-litellm` packages installed, an unauthenticated attacker can force the server to make an outbound HTTP request to an arbitrary host of their choosing, carrying attacker-controlled headers (SSRF).

### Details
`Scorer.model_validate_json()` reflects a class name from a JSON payload behind an import-path allowlist that never constrains the reflected attribute or its kwargs, in `mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py:549-604`:

```python
data = serialized.third_party_scorer_data          # attacker JSON
module_path = data.get("module") or ""
class_name = data.get("class")
if not any(module_path == m or module_path.startswith(m + ".")
           for m in THIRD_PARTY_SCORER_ALLOWED_MODULES):
    raise MlflowException.invalid_parameter_value(...)
module = importlib.import_module(module_path)
scorer_class = getattr(module, class_name, None)   # attribute NOT constrained
...
init_kwargs: dict[str, Any] = dict(data.get("kwargs") or {})  # kwargs NOT constrained
...
init_kwargs["model"] = data["model"]               # attacker model URI
scorer_instance = scorer_class(**init_kwargs)      # reflective instantiation
```

The allowlist (`mlflow/genai/scorers/scorer_utils.py:46-51`) only gates the import path:

```python
THIRD_PARTY_SCORER_ALLOWED_MODULES = frozenset({
    "mlflow.genai.scorers.ragas",
    "mlflow.genai.scorers.deepeval",
    "mlflow.genai.scorers.trulens",
    "mlflow.genai.scorers.phoenix",
})
```

findings.title: filelock: SoftFileLock evicts a fresh lock file whose watched age another local user's pre-dated file passed on through inode reuse
findings.summary:
`SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` evict an unparsable marker (the lock file at `<path>`, whose presence says a process holds the lock) once a waiting contender has watched it unchanged for two seconds. `SoftFileLease` expires a lease the same way. The watch tells two looks apart by the marker's modification time (mtime) and inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) alone.

Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky `/tmp` included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), parks an empty file of its own at the lock path. It dates that file to a future tick of the kernel's coarse clock (a clock that advances in steps of 4 ms), lets the waiters of the user running the lock (the lock user below) watch it past two seconds, and unlinks it in that tick. On a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight back (ext4, overlayfs on ext4) the lock user's next marker repeats both values. It inherits the time spent watching the other user's file, and a second waiter removes it while its owner holds the lock.

Two of the lock user's processes then run the critical section together with no error. A `SoftFileLease` waiter takes a live lease that its owner wrote moments before, within milliseconds instead of after `lease_duration`. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.1.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-RKC48J5B`).

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N, 4.7 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): a race the other user cannot steer. It needs ext4-style inode reuse, a coarse-clock timestamp tick the other user can predict, and two polls of the lock user inside a 4 ms tick and a ~75 µs create-to-write gap. The scanner measured 2 to 10 % of attempts; none of our own 250 attempts fired. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interac

findings.title: filelock: SoftFileLock stale-break restore follows a swapped-in symbolic link and hard-links a file of the user running the lock into the lock directory
findings.summary:
When a soft-lock stale break finds that the marker (the lock file at `<path>`) it renamed aside was a live one recreated by a successor, the restore branch of `break_lock_file()` checks the break name with `lstat` (a check that reads a name without following a symbolic link) and then calls `os.link(break_path, lock_file)` by name. On CPython 3.12 and later on Linux (and on macOS) that call follows a symbolic link (a file that redirects to another path). A local user (the other user below) who can write a shared lock directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it) replaces the break name with a symbolic link between those two calls.

The `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease` or `lifetime` break of the user running the lock (the lock user below) then creates a hard link (a second name for the same file), in that directory, to any of the lock user's own files on the same filesystem. That includes files inside directories the other user cannot enter and links that `fs.protected_hardlinks` (a Linux setting that forbids hard links to files one does not own) refuses the other user when it asks itself. The link exposes the file's size, times, mode and owner, keeps the inode (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) alive, and gives the other user a name it can move. On 4.2.0 a later `FileLock` of the lock user on that name truncated the file. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.1.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-SB29HIAL`).

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N, 5.3 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): two short races against a few lines of Python, timed by inotify (a Linux facility that reports file events), and the lock user must take the lock again and again (the scanner won 10 runs out of 10 after 9 to 910 lock cycles). `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no

findings.title: Pillow: Arrow export leaks stale heap memory when PILLOW_ALIGNMENT > 1
findings.summary:
### Summary

When [`PILLOW_ALIGNMENT`](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/block_allocator.html#memory-pools) is set above 1, exporting an image to Arrow returns uninitialized heap memory mixed in with the pixel data. That memory can include pixels from images the process freed earlier. 

### Details

With an alignment above 1, the default allocator pads each row up to `aligned_linesize` and starts the first row at an aligned offset into the block. It then exports `im->blocks[0].ptr` as `xsize * ysize` tightly packed pixels, so exported data includes the padding bytes, and can include a few bytes from before the first row.

Tested vulnerable on 11.2.1, 12.3.0, 4c1ed27a5.

### PoC

Whether things leak may depend on allocator configuration. This does show a leak on my Mac.

```python
import os

os.environ["PILLOW_ALIGNMENT"] = "64"

from PIL import Image

# Image A: 64 px wide, so its rows fill the whole aligned stride
a = Image.new("L", (64, 40), 0x41).transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)
del a

# Image B: 61 px wide, so each row has 3 bytes of padding; its pixels are all 0
b = Image.new("L", (61, 40), 0).transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)

try:
    exported = Image.fromarrow(b, b.mode, b.size).tobytes()
except ValueError as e:
    print("Not vulnerable:", e)
else:
    if leaked := len(exported) - exported.count(0):
        raise RuntimeError(f"{leaked} of {len(exported)} exported bytes are not B's pixels")
```

### Impact

Information disclosure for applications that set `PILLOW_ALIGNMENT` and export images to Arrow. Likely any image whose row length isn't a multiple of the alignment will do. In a service handling several users' images, one user's exported data can contain pixels from another user's image, or other stale heap contents.

findings.title: odf-kit has HTML injection leading to XSS in odsToHtml() via unescaped style attribute values
findings.summary:
### Summary

ODF style values are interpolated into `style="..."` attributes without HTML-escaping in odf-kit's ODS to-HTML renderer (`odsToHtml()`). A double-quote character inside an attacker-controlled style value breaks out of the attribute, allowing arbitrary HTML/attribute injection — and therefore script execution (XSS) — from a crafted `.ods` file wherever the rendered output is inserted as HTML, which is the documented purpose of the function.

### Details

Two emission sites in `src/ods/to-html/html-renderer.ts` (before 0.14.0, `src/ods-reader/html-renderer.ts`) write document-controlled values into a `style` attribute without escaping:

- **Cell style.** `buildInlineStyle()` assembles a CSS string from the cell's formatting properties (`fo:color`, `fo:font-size`, `fo:font-family`, `fo:background-color`, `fo:text-align`, etc.) with no escaping, and `renderCell` emits it raw as the cell's `style` attribute.
- **Row height.** `row.height` (from `style:row-height`) is emitted raw into the row element's `style` attribute.

The same defect in the ODT renderer (`odtToHtml()`) is tracked as GHSA-3cgg-c5pp-57h6 (CVE-2026-113787).

### Impact

Any consumer that renders `odsToHtml()` output as HTML gets XSS from a crafted `.ods` file they convert: untrusted file → arbitrary tags and attributes → script execution in the host page with the page's origin.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.14.2. Both sites now route document-controlled values through a shared attribute-escaping helper:

- [`1424227`](https://github.com/GitHubNewbie0/odf-kit/commit/1424227d1ca2716a249b623d1456575ff0331dcc): escape style attribute values in the ODS HTML renderer
- [`aa64c73`](https://github.com/GitHubNewbie0/odf-kit/commit/aa64c734ebd7e7be40e35fcda83b1144193c3da2): the shared `escapeAttr` helper

Users should upgrade to 0.14.2 or later.

### Credit

Reported by @PethuKannan.

findings.title: Strands Agents SDK: Exposure of data element to wrong session in the A2A Server
findings.summary:
**Summary**  
Strands Agents SDK is an open-source SDK, available for Python (strands-agents) and TypeScript (@strands-agents/sdk), for building and running AI agents. An issue exists where, under certain circumstances, the Agent2Agent (A2A) server shares conversation history across callers with different context\_id values, allowing one caller to read and influence another caller's session.  
  
**Impact**  
The A2A server did not properly isolate conversation state between callers. In multi-tenant deployments, an authenticated remote user could access another caller's conversation history or influence model behavior for other callers (CWE-488: Unintended Disclosure of Data Element to Wrong Session). This affects any deployment where an A2A server is reachable by more than one user or tenant.  
  
**Impacted versions:**  
strands-agents (Python): all versions containing the multiagent.a2a module, < 1.43.0  
@strands-agents/sdk (TypeScript): < 1.5.0  
  
**Patches**  
This issue has been addressed in strands-agents version 1.43.0 and @strands-agents/sdk version 1.5.0. The A2A server now uses an agent factory so conversation state is isolated per A2A context\_id. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.  
  
**Workarounds**  
There is no workaround that fully addresses this issue in affected versions. Until you upgrade, do not expose an A2A server to more than one user or tenant. If multiple callers need access, run a separate A2A server instance for each user or tenant.  
  
**References**  
If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, we ask that you contact AWS Security via our [vulnerability reporting page](https://aws.amazon.com/security/vulnerability-reporting) or directly via email to [aws-security@amazon.com](mailto:aws-security@amazon.com). Please do not create a public GitHub issue.

findings.title: Twisted: Denial of Service in the Twisted IMAP4 Server via a Negative Literal Size in SEARCH
findings.summary:
## Summary

An infinite-loop vulnerability (CWE-835) in the Twisted IMAP4 server lets an authenticated client freeze the whole process with one small command. `twisted.mail.imap4.parseNestedParens` reads an IMAP literal size with `int()` and never rejects a negative value. A negative size such as `{-100}` drives the parser cursor negative, and because a negative Python index wraps around the end of the string instead of raising, the scanning loop never terminates. It runs synchronously on the single-threaded reactor, so one `SEARCH` command holds the reactor at full CPU forever and every other connection stops being served.

## Details

Meeting an inline literal, `parseNestedParens` reads the size between the braces and advances the cursor past the body:

```python
# twisted/mail/imap4.py  parseNestedParens
literalSize = int(s[i + 1 : end])          # no sign check
contentStack[-1].append((s[end + 3 : end + 3 + literalSize],))
i = end + 3 + literalSize                    # negative size -> i goes negative
```

`int(b"-100")` is `-100`, so `i` goes negative; the loop condition `i < len(s)` stays true and `s[i : i + 1]` on a negative index never raises, so the cursor cycles forever. The `_literalStringLimit` guard only covers the synchronizing-literal continuation path, not this inline branch. The call is reached from `select_SEARCH` through `arg_searchkeys`, dispatched only in the selected state, so a valid login and a selected mailbox (any low-privilege account) suffice. It runs in the reactor thread, and the connection timeout cannot fire because the reactor itself is frozen.

Affected product: Twisted (`twisted.mail`), the IMAP4 server `twisted.mail.imap4.IMAP4Server`
Affected versions: 26.4.0 and earlier

## PoC

Log in, select a mailbox, and send a `SEARCH` whose literal size is negative:

```text
C: t1 LOGIN testuser password-test
C: t2 SELECT INBOX
C: t3 SEARCH {-100}zzzzzzzzzz
```

The server never responds and one core stays at 100 percent. In a measured run

findings.title: Twisted: Unauthenticated Remote Denial of Service in the Twisted conch Telnet Transport via an Unbounded Subnegotiation Buffer
findings.summary:
## Summary

An allocation-without-limits vulnerability (CWE-770) in the Twisted conch telnet transport lets any unauthenticated remote peer exhaust server memory over a single connection. When the peer opens a telnet subnegotiation with `IAC SB` and then streams bytes without ever sending the `IAC SE` terminator, every byte is appended to a per-connection buffer that has no maximum length. The buffer persists across reads and is released only on the terminator the attacker withholds, so it grows without bound until the process is killed.

## Details

The option-negotiation state machine in `Telnet.dataReceived` enters the `subnegotiation` state on `IAC SB` and sets an empty command list. In that state every non-`IAC` byte is appended to the list with no length check:

```python
# src/twisted/conch/telnet.py  (Telnet.dataReceived)
elif self.state == "subnegotiation":
    if b == IAC:
        self.state = "subnegotiation-escaped"
    else:
        self.commands.append(b)      # unbounded: no len(self.commands) check
```

`self.commands` is an instance attribute that persists across `dataReceived` calls and is deleted only when `IAC SE` completes the subnegotiation. Negotiation runs at the transport layer before authentication, and the bytes are consumed inside `dataReceived` before any application callback, so an application cannot impose a bound. Twisted caps other parser buffers, for example `NetstringReceiver.MAX_LENGTH`, but not this one.

Affected product: Twisted, `twisted.conch.telnet` transport
Affected versions: confirmed against 26.4.0

## PoC

On any endpoint that exposes the Twisted telnet transport, such as the Twisted manhole telnet service, open one connection and send the two bytes `IAC SB` (`0xFF 0xFA`), then stream any non-`0xFF` bytes continuously and never send the `IAC SE` terminator (`0xFF 0xF0`). No credentials are required, because option negotiation runs before authentication.

Every byte is appended to the per-connection subnegotiation buffer

findings.title: Bringing Rust to the Pixel Baseband
findings.summary: Posted by Jiacheng Lu, Software Engineer, Google Pixel Team Google is continuously advancing the security of Pixel devices. We have been focusing on hardening the cellular baseband modem against exploitation. Recognizing the risks associated within the complex modem firmware, Pixel 9 shipped with mitigations against a range of memory-safety vulnerabilities. For Pixel 10, Google is advancing its proactive security measures further. Following our previous discussion on "Deploying Rust in Existing Firmware Codebases" , this post shares a concrete application: integrating a memory-safe Rust DNS(Domain Name System) parser into the modem firmware. The new Rust-based DNS parser significantly reduces our security risk by mitigating an entire class of vulnerabilities in a risky area, while also laying the foundation for broader adoption of memory-safe code in other areas. Here we share our experience of working on it, and hope it can inspire the use of more memory safe languages in low-level environments. Why Modem Memory Safety Can’t Wait In recent years, we have seen increasing interest in the cellular modem from attackers and security researchers. For example, Google's Project Zero gained remote code execution on Pixel modems over the Internet. Pixel modem has tens of Megabytes of executable code. Given the complexity and remote attack surface of the modem, other critical memory safety vulnerabilities may remain in the predominantly memory-unsafe firmware code. Why DNS? The DNS protocol is most commonly known in the context of browsers finding websites. With the evolution of cellular technology, modern cellular communications have migrated to digital data networks; consequently, even basic operations such as call forwarding rely on DNS services. DNS is a complex protocol and requires parsing of untrusted data, which can lead to vulnerabilities, particularly when implemented in a memory-unsafe language (example: CVE-2024-27227 ).
